responses.content:
The Chandrasekhar limit is the maximum mass that a stable white dwarf star can have while supporting itself against gravitational collapse through electron degeneracy pressure. This limit is approximately 1.4 times the mass of the Sun (about \(1.4 M_{\odot}\)). It is named after the Indian-American astrophysicist Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar, who calculated this critical mass in the early 20th century.

When a white dwarf's mass approaches this limit, electron degeneracy pressure is no longer sufficient to counteract the gravitational forces, and the star can collapse further, potentially leading to a supernova or forming a neutron star or black hole, depending on the circumstances. This concept is crucial in understanding the life cycle of stars, particularly those of intermediate mass.

## CORRECT ANSWER
The Chandrasekhar limit is the maximum mass that a stable white dwarf star can have while supporting itself against gravitational collapse through electron degeneracy pressure. This limit is approximately 1.4 times the mass of the Sun (about \(1.4 M_{\odot}\)). It was calculated by the Indian-American astrophysicist Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar in the early 20th century. When a white dwarf's mass approaches this limit, electron degeneracy pressure becomes insufficient to counteract gravitational forces, leading the star to potentially undergo further collapse, which can result in a supernova or the formation of a neutron star, although white dwarfs do not directly collapse into black holes.
